headings.text: 📋 At a glance: the tell → the principle

notes.html:
What to have in your head before designing a single class. Note 01 gives you the four tools; note 02 gives the rules for using them so change stays cheap; note 03 gives the brakes; note 04 turns a requirement into one pattern. Read each arrow as a sentence: OOP is disciplined by SOLID, which is restrained by DRY, KISS, YAGNI, which leaves room for the one pattern the requirement needs.

Green = CORE notes in this folder, grey = other sections (dashed edges).

Reading order:01 OOP: the four pillars02 SOLID03 DRY, KISS, YAGNI04 the pattern selector

Owners

Ideas several notes touch, and the one note that explains each. Every other note links instead of re-explaining.

Idea Owner note
Encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism: what each is for, in Java and Python 01 OOP
Encapsulation vs abstraction; overloading vs overriding; interface vs abstract class 01 OOP
The five SOLID principles, each as a violation and a fix 02 SOLID
What "one responsibility" means; the Liskov rules; inversion vs injection vs a container 02 SOLID
Duplicated knowledge vs coincidental duplication; the rule of three; the wrong abstraction 03 DRY, KISS, YAGNI
When an abstraction is justified (SOLID against YAGNI) 03 DRY, KISS, YAGNI
From the interviewer's sentence to one pattern 04 pattern selector
One three-line violation per SOLID letter, as a recognition drill item 6, not these notes
Open/closed as what the round is scored on item 7, not these notes
Composition in place of inheritance, worked through item 8, not these notes
Law of Demeter; tell, don't ask item 9, not these notes
Protecting a state machine with intent methods; the anemic model item 10 and item 11, not these notes
Small interfaces as the knobs follow-ups turn; constructor injection in practice item 12 and item 13, not these notes
Each pattern, and when patterns are too much §3 design patterns and pattern overuse, not these notes
How Java resolves overloads and overrides OOP pillars and dispatch traps, not these notes

Decision trees

No tree of its own: the principles here are not alternatives to choose between, they are checks you run together. The two real choices have their trees elsewhere: "should I add this abstraction?" in note 03, and "which pattern?" in the pattern selector. What this section needs is a lookup from what you see to what it is called.

At a glance: the tell → the principle

What you see in the code Principle it breaks The fix Note
a public field, or a setter anyone can call encapsulation private state, intent methods that can refuse 01
callers depend on a concrete class and its details abstraction an interface the caller owns 01
if / switch on a type or enum, repeated polymorphism, open/closed one class per case behind an interface 01, 02
a subclass that exists only to reuse the parent's code inheritance misuse hold the other object in a field 01
"and" in the class's description; unrelated edits collide single responsibility split by who asks for the change 02
an override that throws, does nothing, or changes meaning Liskov substitution no inheritance; a shared interface 02
UnsupportedOperationException; empty method bodies interface segregation several small interfaces 02
new ConcreteThing() inside business logic dependency inversion constructor injection 02
one rule change needs the same edit in several files DRY give the rule one home 03
ten files to trace one request; patterns with one case KISS the plainest design that meets the requirement 03
parameters, options or layers nothing uses YAGNI delete them; build when asked 03
a shared helper with boolean flags per caller DRY over-applied inline, then extract only what is truly common 03

Four bullets

  • The one big idea: every principle here serves one goal, that a change in requirements touches one small place. OOP supplies the mechanisms, SOLID says where to put the seams, and DRY, KISS and YAGNI stop you adding seams nobody asked for.
  • The two most-confused pairs: encapsulation vs abstraction (01: hiding state behind rules vs hiding the implementation behind a contract) · open/closed vs YAGNI (02 and 03: add the seam where the requirement names a variation, not the implementations).
  • Ten minutes before an interview: the table above, note 01's class diagram, note 02's OrderService diagram, note 03's "should I add this abstraction?" flow, and the pattern selector's lookup.
  • Cross-section links: these principles are applied to real problems in ../../07-Design-problems/; thread-safety, which none of these notes cover, is §4 concurrency in LLD. Content gaps (no note yet): cohesion and coupling as measures; GRASP; the Law of Demeter has a note, but "separation of concerns" as a principle does not.

notes.title: OOP — Encapsulation, Abstraction, Inheritance, Polymorphism

headings.text: 1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)
4. The whole example — Java then Python
5. ① Encapsulation — guard your own state
6. ② Abstraction — show what, hide how
8. ④ Polymorphism — one call, many behaviours

notes.html:
This note has one job: make the four pillars something you use while designing classes, not four definitions you recite. Each pillar is shown as the problem it removes, on one small payments example, in Java and then Python.

Reference Links

  • Java's own framing of the concepts — Oracle Java Tutorials: Object-Oriented Programming Concepts · Interfaces and Inheritance
  • Python's class model — Python tutorial: Classes · abc: abstract base classes · PEP 544: Protocols (structural subtyping)
  • Behaviour belongs with the data — Martin Fowler: TellDontAsk

REVISION BLOCK

1. Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The four pillars, each in four words? Encapsulation: guard your own state. Abstraction: show what, hide how. Inheritance: share by being-a. Polymorphism: one call, many behaviours.
Encapsulation vs abstraction? Encapsulation hides state behind rules. Abstraction hides implementation behind a contract.
Overloading vs overriding? Overloading: same name, different parameters, chosen at compile time. Overriding: subclass replaces a method, chosen at run time.
When is inheritance the wrong tool? When the relationship is "has a" or "uses a", or the subclass can't honour every promise of the parent.
How does Python do the same things? _name and properties; ABC or Protocol; ordinary subclassing; duck typing.
Draw by hand: the payments class diagram PaymentMethod interface on top; Wallet and abstract CardPayment implement it; CreditCard, DebitCard extend CardPayment; checkout calls only the interface.

2. Interview Explanation (30 Seconds)

Object-oriented design rests on four ideas. Encapsulation keeps an object's state private and lets it change only through methods that enforce its rules. Abstraction exposes what something does through an interface and hides how. Inheritance lets a subclass reuse and specialise a parent, and is only right for a true "is-a". Polymorphism lets one call site work with any implementation, so new behaviour arrives as a new class and not a new if. In an LLD round, encapsulation protects invariants and polymorphism is what makes the "now add X" follow-up cheap.

3. At a glance

Pillar The question it answers The tell that it's missing Java Python
Encapsulation who is allowed to change this state? public fields or setters; rules checked by callers private fields, intent methods _name, @property without a setter
Abstraction what does a caller need to know? callers depend on a concrete class and its details interface, abstract class Protocol, ABC
Inheritance what is truly shared by a family? copy-pasted steps across sibling classes extends, abstract methods subclassing, @abstractmethod
Polymorphism how does one call do different things? if/switch on a type or an enum, repeated overriding, interfaces duck typing, overriding

The four on one small model. Checkout only ever sees the interface.

Dashed arrows with a hollow head mean implements; solid ones mean extends. Read it as four statements: Wallet hides its balance (①), PaymentMethod is all that Checkout knows (②), the two cards share pay and differ only in fee (③), and Checkout calls pay without knowing which class answers (④).

4. The whole example — Java then Python

The numbers ①–④ mark where each pillar appears. Both programs were compiled and run.

import java.util.List;

interface PaymentMethod {                              // ② abstraction: what it does, not how
    void pay(long paise);
    String name();
}

class Wallet implements PaymentMethod {                // ① encapsulation: state plus the rules that guard it
    private long balancePaise;                         // private, and no setter
    Wallet(long openingPaise) { this.balancePaise = openingPaise; }

    public void topUp(long paise) {
        if (paise <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("top-up must be positive");
        balancePaise += paise;
    }
    @Override public void pay(long paise) {
        if (paise > balancePaise) throw new IllegalStateException("insufficient balance");
        balancePaise -= paise;                         // the only way the balance goes down
    }
    @Override public String name() { return "wallet"; }
    public long balance() { return balancePaise; }
}

abstract class CardPayment implements PaymentMethod {  // ③ inheritance: shared steps written once
    protected final String last4;
    CardPayment(String last4) { this.last4 = last4; }
    @Override public void pay(long paise) {
        System.out.println(name() + " ****" + last4 + " charged " + (paise + fee(paise)));
    }
    protected abstract long fee(long paise);           // the one step that differs
}
class CreditCard extends CardPayment {
    CreditCard(String last4) { super(last4); }
    @Override protected long fee(long paise) { return paise * 2 / 100; }
    @Override public String name() { return "credit card"; }
}
class DebitCard extends CardPayment {
    DebitCard(String last4) { super(last4); }
    @Override protected long fee(long paise) { return 0; }
    @Override public String name() { return "debit card"; }
}

public class OopDemo {
    static void checkout(PaymentMethod method, long paise) { method.pay(paise); }   // ④ polymorphism

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Wallet wallet = new Wallet(50_000);
        List<PaymentMethod> methods = List.of(wallet, new CreditCard("4242"), new DebitCard("1881"));
        for (PaymentMethod m : methods) checkout(m, 10_000);
        System.out.println("wallet balance " + wallet.balance());
    }
}
// → credit card ****4242 charged 10200
// → debit card ****1881 charged 10000
// → wallet balance 40000

The Python version says the same four things in Python's own idiom. It is not Java with different punctuation.

from abc import ABC, abstractmethod
from typing import Protocol

class PaymentMethod(Protocol):                 # ② abstraction: a structural type; no base class required
    def pay(self, paise: int) -> None: ...

class Wallet:                                  # ① encapsulation: by convention, enforced with a property
    def __init__(self, opening_paise: int) -> None:
        self._balance = opening_paise          # leading underscore: internal
    @property
    def balance(self) -> int:                  # readable; no setter is defined
        return self._balance
    def top_up(self, paise: int) -> None:
        if paise <= 0:
            raise ValueError("top-up must be positive")
        self._balance += paise
    def pay(self, paise: int) -> None:
        if paise > self._balance:
            raise RuntimeError("insufficient balance")
        self._balance -= paise

class CardPayment(ABC):                        # ③ inheritance: shared steps in the parent
    name = "card"
    def __init__(self, last4: str) -> None:
        self.last4 = last4
    def pay(self, paise: int) -> None:
        print(f"{self.name} ****{self.last4} charged {paise + self.fee(paise)}")
    @abstractmethod
    def fee(self, paise: int) -> int: ...

class CreditCard(CardPayment):
    name = "credit card"
    def fee(self, paise: int) -> int:
        return paise * 2 // 100

class DebitCard(CardPayment):
    name = "debit card"
    def fee(self, paise: int) -> int:
        return 0

def checkout(method: PaymentMethod, paise: int) -> None:   # ④ polymorphism: anything with pay() works
    method.pay(paise)

wallet = Wallet(50_000)
for m in (wallet, CreditCard("4242"), DebitCard("1881")):
    checkout(m, 10_000)
print("wallet balance", wallet.balance)
# → credit card ****4242 charged 10200
# → debit card ****1881 charged 10000
# → wallet balance 40000

Note what Python did not need: Wallet never mentions PaymentMethod. It has a pay method, so it fits. That is structural typing, and it is the main difference between the two languages in this note.

5. ① Encapsulation — guard your own state

The problem it removes. Make balancePaise public and any code anywhere can write wallet.balancePaise -= amount. Now the rule "a balance never goes negative" has to be remembered at every call site, and the first one that forgets creates a negative balance nobody can trace.

What it is. The object owns its state and the rules about that state. Callers don't set fields; they ask for an outcome (pay, topUp) and the object decides whether it is allowed. This is "tell, don't ask".

Java Python
Hide the field private long balancePaise; self._balance (a convention; __balance name-mangles)
Read-only access a getter and no setter @property with no setter
What stops a bad write the compiler: the field is not visible AttributeError at run time for the property; nothing for _balance

In Java wallet.balancePaise = -1 does not compile. In Python wallet.balance = -1 raises AttributeError, while wallet._balance = -1 works: Python relies on convention, so the property and the intent methods are the real protection.

A getter and a setter for every field is not encapsulation. It is a public field with extra typing. The test: can an outsider put the object into an invalid state? If yes, it isn't encapsulated. Protecting state transitions in a design is taken further in encapsulation of invariants.

6. ② Abstraction — show what, hide how

The problem it removes. If checkout code calls creditCard.contactBank() and wallet.deduct(), it knows how every payment works. Every new payment type means editing checkout.

What it is. A contract that says what can be done (pay) and nothing about how. The caller depends on the contract; implementations can change or multiply behind it.

Java Python
A pure contract interface Protocol (checked by a type checker, structural)
A contract with shared code abstract class ABC with @abstractmethod
Enforcement compile time: a class must implement every method ABC: TypeError on instantiation. Protocol: only the type checker

Choose an interface when implementations share nothing but the contract (Wallet and a card have no common code). Choose an abstract class when they share real steps (CardPayment.pay). A class can implement many interfaces and extend one class, so the interface is the safer default.

Encapsulation and abstraction are often confused. Encapsulation is about one object protecting its data. Abstraction is about a caller not needing to know which object it has.

7. ③ Inheritance — share by being-a

The problem it removes. Credit and debit cards both mask the number, add a fee and charge. Written twice, the two copies drift apart.

What it is. The parent holds the shared state and the shared steps; each child supplies only what differs. Here CardPayment.pay is written once and fee is the single hook. (That shape, fixed steps with one overridable step, is the template method pattern.)

The rule for using it: "is-a", and every promise kept. A CreditCard is a CardPayment in every situation, so inheritance fits. If a subclass has to disable or weaken something the parent promises, it is not a subtype, however similar the code looks. That is the Liskov rule, covered in SOLID.

Inheritance gives you It costs you
reuse of state and behaviour with no delegation code the tightest coupling there is: a change to the parent reaches every child
a ready-made polymorphic family one parent only in Java; a fixed hierarchy that the next requirement may not fit

When the relationship is "has a" or "uses a" (a Checkout has a payment method; an Order has a discount rule), hold the other object in a field and call it. That is composition, and it is the default in LLD: see composition over inheritance. Python allows multiple inheritance and resolves methods by the MRO (ClassName.__mro__); keep it to small mixins.

8. ④ Polymorphism — one call, many behaviours

The problem it removes. Without it, checkout looks like this, and so does every other place that touches a payment:

if (type.equals("WALLET")) { /* deduct */ }
else if (type.equals("CREDIT")) { /* charge + 2% */ }
else if (type.equals("DEBIT")) { /* charge */ }     // a new method edits every such chain

What it is. method.pay(paise) is one line. Which pay runs is decided at run time by the object's actual class. Adding UPI is a new class; checkout doesn't change. This is the mechanism behind open/closed and behind most design patterns.

Two different things share the name, and interviewers ask about the difference:

Overriding (run-time polymorphism) Overloading (compile-time)
What it is a subclass replaces a parent's method several methods with one name and different parameters
Chosen by the actual object, at run time the declared types of the arguments, at compile time
Python yes, the normal case no: a second def replaces the first; use default arguments or functools.singledispatch 
class Printer {
    void print(Object o) { System.out.println("object"); }
    void print(String s) { System.out.println("string"); }
}
Object x = "hello";
new Printer().print(x);                    // → object       overload picked from the declared type, Object
PaymentMethod m = new CreditCard("4242");
System.out.println(m.name());              // → credit card  override picked from the real object

In Python, polymorphism needs no declared relationship at all: any object with a pay method works in checkout. That freedom is why a Protocol is worth writing down: it documents the contract that duck typing otherwise leaves implicit.

9. Interview Follow-ups

Q · Mechanism — What is the difference between an abstract class and an interface, and when do you use each?

An interface is a pure contract: method signatures a class promises to provide. An abstract class is a partly built class: it can hold fields, constructors and finished methods, and leaves some methods for subclasses. Use an interface when unrelated classes need to be used the same way and share no code. Use an abstract class when a family shares real state or steps. A Java class can implement many interfaces and extend only one class, so a design that starts with interfaces keeps more options open. Java interfaces can carry default methods, which narrows the gap, but they still can't hold instance state.

Q · Trade-off — Inheritance or composition for adding behaviour to a class?

Inheritance when the new class is a true subtype that keeps every promise of the parent and the variation is along one axis. Composition otherwise, which is most of the time. The trouble with inheritance shows on the second requirement: cards vary by fee, and then also by network, and then by reward scheme, and a hierarchy can only split along one of those. With composition each varying part is its own small object held in a field (FeePolicy, RewardPolicy), and they combine freely. Inheritance also exposes the parent's internals to the child, so parent changes break children.

Q · Failure — A Stack class extends ArrayList to reuse its storage. What goes wrong?

It inherits every public method of the list, including add(index, element) and remove(index), so any caller can insert into the middle of the stack and break last-in-first-out order. The class can't protect its own invariant, because inheritance published the parent's whole interface. You would confirm it by writing a test that inserts at index 0. The fix is composition: the stack has a list in a private field and exposes only push, pop and peek. This is why java.util.Stack extending Vector is cited as a design mistake.

Q · Design — Model notifications for an app that sends email and SMS today and will add push and WhatsApp.

The plural in the requirement is the axis of change, so that is where the abstraction goes: a NotificationChannel interface with one send(recipient, message) method, and one class per channel. Callers hold a list of channels and loop; they never branch on a channel type. Each channel encapsulates its own credentials and rate limits. I would not build a class hierarchy of channels: they share a contract, not code. If two channels later share retry logic, that goes in a helper object they both hold. Adding WhatsApp is then one new class and one line of wiring. The requirement-to-pattern step is in the pattern selector.

Pitfalls

  • Not the same: encapsulation vs abstraction
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both are described as "hiding", and many textbooks define each using the other.
    ↳ Difference: encapsulation hides an object's state behind methods that enforce its rules. Abstraction hides which implementation you are talking to behind a contract.
    ↳ Think instead: private balance plus pay() is encapsulation; PaymentMethod is abstraction. You can have either without the other.
  • "Private fields with getters and setters means the class is encapsulated"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: IDEs generate them, frameworks expect them, and the fields are technically private.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: a setter lets any caller put the object into any state, so every rule about that state lives outside the class. That is a public field with ceremony.
    ↳ Think instead: expose intent, not fields. reserve(), pay(), cancel(): methods that can refuse.
  • "Inheritance is how you reuse code"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it is the first reuse mechanism every OOP course teaches, and it saves typing immediately.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: it couples the child to the parent's internals and publishes the parent's whole interface, wanted or not (the Stack extends ArrayList failure).
    ↳ Think instead: inheritance is for subtyping: a real "is-a" that keeps every promise. For reuse alone, hold the other object in a field.
  • Not the same: overloading vs overriding
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: similar words, and both are sometimes called polymorphism.
    ↳ Difference: overloading picks a method from the arguments' declared types at compile time; overriding picks from the object's actual class at run time.
    ↳ Think instead: only overriding lets new classes change behaviour without touching callers. Overloading is a naming convenience. Python has no overloading at all.
  • Don't branch on type when a method would do.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: an if on an enum or instanceof is quick to write and easy to read the first time.
    ↳ What goes wrong: the same chain reappears wherever the type matters, and each new type means finding and editing all of them.
    ↳ Do instead: put the varying behaviour in a method on the type and call it. One if in a factory that creates the object is fine.
  • Don't write Java in Python.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the Java version of a design is the one in most books and interview answers.
    ↳ What goes wrong: you get getter and setter methods, single-method classes and deep ABC trees where a property, a function and a Protocol would be clearer.
    ↳ Do instead: a @property for controlled access, a plain callable for a one-method strategy, a Protocol for a contract.

Connections

  • Next: the rules for using these four well — SOLID. Each letter is a discipline on one of the pillars.
  • Keeping designs small — DRY, KISS, YAGNI.
  • Encapsulation, in a design problem — encapsulation of invariants shows it protecting a booking's state machine; anemic domain model is what its absence looks like.
  • Inheritance, and its alternative — composition over inheritance.
  • Polymorphism, as patterns — strategy and state are polymorphism given a name; the pattern selector says when to reach for each.
  • The language underneath — OOP pillars and dispatch traps (Java): how Java resolves overloads and overrides, with the traps.

notes.title: SOLID — Five Principles, Each as a Violation and Its Fix

headings.text: 1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)
4. The starting point — one method, three violations

notes.html:
This note has one job: explain each principle well enough that you can spot its violation in code you are shown and fix it out loud. The short recognition drill, one three-line violation per letter, is item 6; this is the explanation behind it.

Reference Links

  • The principles, restated by their author with what each is for — Robert C. Martin: Solid Relevance
  • The original catalogue — Robert C. Martin: The Principles of OOD
  • How Python expresses an interface — PEP 544: Protocols

REVISION BLOCK

1. Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The five, one line each? S: one reason to change. O: add by adding, not editing. L: a subtype keeps every promise. I: small interfaces per caller. D: depend on abstractions, injected.
What does "responsibility" mean in SRP? A reason to change: one actor, one stakeholder whose request would edit the class.
The tell for an OCP violation? An if or switch over a type or category that grows with each new requirement.
LSP's classic violation, and why? Square extends Rectangle: code that sets width 5 and height 4 expects area 20 and gets 16.
The tell for an ISP violation? An implementation that throws "unsupported" or leaves a method empty.
Draw by hand: OrderService after the fix OrderService in the middle, arrows out to three interfaces: DiscountPolicy, OrderRepository, Notifier; implementations hang under each.

2. Interview Explanation (30 Seconds)

SOLID is five rules for keeping change cheap. Single responsibility: a class has one reason to change. Open/closed: new behaviour comes as a new class, not an edit to working code. Liskov substitution: anything written against a parent type must still work with any subtype. Interface segregation: callers depend on small interfaces that match what they use. Dependency inversion: business logic depends on abstractions, and concrete classes are passed in. In a design round the two that are scored are open/closed and dependency inversion, because every follow-up is "now add X".

3. At a glance

Says The tell that it's violated The fix
S · Single responsibility one class, one reason to change "and" in the class's description; unrelated edits collide in one file split by who asks for the change
O · Open/closed open to extension, closed to modification an if/switch on a type that grows an interface, and one class per case
L · Liskov substitution subtypes are usable wherever the parent is an override that throws, does nothing, or changes meaning don't inherit; share an interface
I · Interface segregation no caller depends on methods it doesn't use UnsupportedOperationException; empty methods several small interfaces
D · Dependency inversion high-level code depends on abstractions new ConcreteThing() inside business logic constructor injection of an interface

One class used throughout: an OrderService that checks out an order. Here is where it ends up.

Every arrow leaving OrderService points at an interface. That one property is S, O and D together. A new discount, a new database or a new notification channel is one more box in the bottom row; nothing above it changes.

4. The starting point — one method, three violations

class OrderServiceBefore {
    long checkout(Order order, String customerType) {
        long total = order.subtotalPaise();
        if (customerType.equals("GOLD")) total = total * 90 / 100;         // O: a new tier edits this method
        else if (customerType.equals("SILVER")) total = total * 95 / 100;
        new MySqlOrderRepository().save(order);                            // D: builds its own database class
        System.out.println("<html>Thanks! Total " + total + "</html>");    // S: also writes the email
        return total;
    }
}

It works. The problem is what it costs to change: pricing, storage and email wording all live in one method, so three different people's requests edit the same lines, and it can't be tested without a database.

5. S — Single Responsibility

The question it answers: how many different people can ask for this class to change?

"Responsibility" doesn't mean "does one thing". It means one reason to change, and reasons come from people. In the method above, marketing changes the email, finance changes the discount rules, and the platform team changes the database. Three actors, one class: each edit risks the other two.

The fix is to move each actor's concern behind its own type. OrderService keeps one job, coordinating a checkout; Notifier owns the message and OrderRepository owns storage.

How far to go: split when two parts change for different reasons or at different times. Don't split a class into one-method fragments that always change together: that scatters one responsibility across many files, which is the same problem turned inside out.

6. O — Open/Closed

The question it answers: when a new case arrives, do I add code or edit code?

The if (customerType…) chain is the violation. A platinum tier, a festive offer, a first-order coupon: each one reopens a method that already works and is already tested. The fix is to find what varies (the discount rule), give it an interface, and make each rule a class.

interface DiscountPolicy { long apply(long subtotalPaise); }

class GoldDiscount implements DiscountPolicy { public long apply(long p) { return p * 90 / 100; } }
class FestiveDiscount implements DiscountPolicy { public long apply(long p) { return p - 5_000; } }   // new rule = new class

In Python a one-method interface is just a callable, so a new rule is a new function:

DiscountPolicy = Callable[[int], int]

def gold(paise: int) -> int: return paise * 90 // 100
def festive(paise: int) -> int: return paise - 5_000

checkout now never changes when a rule is added. Somewhere, one place still chooses which policy applies (a factory or a lookup); that single choice point is fine. You can't be closed against every change, so close against the one the requirement names: the plural in "gold, silver and platinum members" tells you where. This is the principle the round is scored on: open/closed as the scoring rubric.

7. L — Liskov Substitution

The question it answers: if I hand this subtype to code written for the parent, does that code still work?

class Rectangle {
    protected int width, height;
    void setWidth(int w) { width = w; }
    void setHeight(int h) { height = h; }
    int area() { return width * height; }
}
class Square extends Rectangle {
    @Override void setWidth(int w) { width = w; height = w; }              // keeps "square", breaks "rectangle"
    @Override void setHeight(int h) { width = h; height = h; }
}

static int stretch(Rectangle r) { r.setWidth(5); r.setHeight(4); return r.area(); }
// stretch(new Rectangle()) → 20
// stretch(new Square())    → 16     same code, different answer

In geometry a square is a rectangle. In code, Rectangle promises that setting the width leaves the height alone, and Square can't keep that promise. stretch did nothing wrong and got the wrong answer. "Is-a" in a design means behaves as, not "is a kind of" in English.

A subtype must:

Rule In plain words
accept everything the parent accepts don't add stricter input checks
deliver everything the parent promises don't return less, or leave state the parent wouldn't
raise nothing the parent's callers don't expect no new "not supported" exceptions

The fix is to stop inheriting. Both are shapes; neither is the other. Making them immutable removes the setters they disagreed about.

interface Shape { int area(); }
record Rect(int width, int height) implements Shape { public int area() { return width * height; } }
record Sq(int side) implements Shape { public int area() { return side * side; } }

class Shape(Protocol):
    def area(self) -> int: ...

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Rect:
    width: int
    height: int
    def area(self) -> int: return self.width * self.height

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Sq:
    side: int
    def area(self) -> int: return self.side ** 2

The same violation in a real design: a ReadOnlyAccount that extends Account and throws on withdraw, or a GiftCard that extends Wallet and rejects topUp. The test is always the same: find a caller of the parent and ask whether it survives.

8. I — Interface Segregation

The question it answers: does this caller have to know about methods it never calls?

interface PaymentMethod { void pay(long paise); void refund(long paise); }

class CashOnDelivery implements PaymentMethod {
    public void pay(long paise) { /* collect at the door */ }
    public void refund(long paise) { throw new UnsupportedOperationException(); }   // the tell
}

Cash on delivery can't refund to a card, yet the interface forces it to pretend. Any code holding a PaymentMethod now has to wonder whether refund will blow up, which is also an L violation: a fat interface is how most Liskov violations get created. The fix is to split the interface by what callers need.

interface Payable { void pay(long paise); }
interface Refundable { void refund(long paise); }

class CardPay implements Payable, Refundable { /* both */ }
class CashOnDelivery implements Payable { /* pay only: no refund method to fake */ }

class Payable(Protocol):
    def pay(self, paise: int) -> None: ...

class Refundable(Protocol):
    def refund(self, paise: int) -> None: ...

def refund_order(method: Refundable, paise: int) -> None:   # asks for exactly what it uses
    method.refund(paise)

Refund code takes a Refundable, so passing cash on delivery is rejected by the compiler (or the type checker) and not discovered at run time. Each small interface is also an extension point for a follow-up: see interface segregation for extension points.

9. D — Dependency Inversion

The question it answers: does my business logic know which database, which email provider, which clock?

new MySqlOrderRepository() inside checkout means the most important code in the system depends on the least stable detail. It can't run in a test without MySQL, and swapping storage means editing business logic. Invert it: the service declares the interface it needs, and the concrete class is handed in.

final class OrderService {
    private final OrderRepository orders;
    private final Notifier notifier;
    OrderService(OrderRepository orders, Notifier notifier) {              // handed in, never new-ed here
        this.orders = orders;
        this.notifier = notifier;
    }
    long checkout(Order order, DiscountPolicy discount) {
        long total = discount.apply(order.subtotalPaise());
        orders.save(order);
        notifier.orderPlaced(order, total);
        return total;
    }
}

InMemoryOrderRepository repo = new InMemoryOrderRepository();
OrderService service = new OrderService(repo, new ConsoleNotifier());
service.checkout(new Order("A2", 100_000), new GoldDiscount());     // → 90000
service.checkout(new Order("A3", 100_000), new FestiveDiscount());  // → 95000
service.checkout(new Order("A4", 100_000), p -> p);                 // → 100000, a lambda is a policy too

class OrderService:
    def __init__(self, orders: OrderRepository, notifier: Notifier) -> None:   # handed in
        self._orders, self._notifier = orders, notifier

    def checkout(self, order: Order, discount: DiscountPolicy) -> int:
        total = discount(order.subtotal_paise)
        self._orders.save(order)
        self._notifier.order_placed(order, total)
        return total

service = OrderService(InMemoryOrderRepository(), ConsoleNotifier())
service.checkout(Order("A2", 100_000), gold)       # → 90000

"Inversion" refers to the direction of the dependency arrow. Before, the service pointed at MySQL. After, both the service and the MySQL class point at OrderRepository, an interface that belongs to the business side. Three related terms: dependency inversion is the principle; dependency injection is the technique (pass it in through the constructor); a DI container such as Spring is a tool that does the passing for you and is not required. More in constructor dependency injection.

10. How the five fit together

If you fix… …you usually also get
O, by extracting an interface for what varies D (the caller now depends on the interface) and a smaller class (S)
I, by splitting a fat interface L (no implementation has to fake a method)
D, by injecting dependencies testability, and the seam O needs

They are five views of one goal: a change in requirements should touch one small place. That is also why they pull against KISS and YAGNI: every interface is a cost, so add one where change is stated or likely, not everywhere.

11. Interview Follow-ups

Q · Mechanism — What exactly is a "single responsibility"? A class with one method?

No. It is one reason to change, and reasons to change come from people. If the finance team, the marketing team and the infrastructure team could each ask for a change that edits the same class, it has three responsibilities, even if it has one method. A class with ten methods that all serve the same stakeholder and change together has one. So the test isn't counting methods; it is asking "who would request a change here, and would they be surprised to break each other's feature?"

Q · Trade-off — Doesn't open/closed mean an interface for everything? Where do you stop?

You can't be closed against every possible change, and trying produces a design nobody can follow. Each interface costs a file, an indirection and a name to learn. So close against the change you have evidence for: a plural in the requirement, a boundary to something external such as a database or payment provider, or a variation you have already had to add twice. Leave the rest concrete. If a new axis of change appears later, extracting an interface from one concrete class is a small refactor, and by then you know its real shape.

Q · Failure — A subclass overrides a method to throw UnsupportedOperationException. Which principle, and what do you do?

Liskov first: code written against the parent calls that method and now fails at run time. Usually interface segregation is the cause: the parent type promised more than every member of the family can do. Confirm it by finding a caller that holds the parent type and calls the method. The fix is to split the capability out: a smaller base type that every member supports, and a separate interface for the optional operation, so code that needs it asks for that interface and the compiler rejects the wrong object.

Q · Design — You are given a 600-line BookingService that prices, books, charges and emails. How do you refactor it under SOLID?

Start with who asks for changes, because that sets the seams: pricing rules, payment, notification and storage are four different owners. Extract an interface at each: PricingPolicy, PaymentGateway, Notifier, BookingRepository, injected through the constructor, with BookingService left as the coordinator of one use case. Do it one seam at a time behind the existing tests, starting with the one that changes most often, usually pricing. I would not split further until a requirement asks: the goal is four clean seams, not forty classes. The first thing to check afterwards is that the service can be unit-tested with in-memory fakes.

Pitfalls

  • "Single responsibility means a class should do only one thing"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the name suggests it, and "do one thing" is the rule for functions.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: taken literally it shreds a design into one-method classes that always change together, so one change now touches five files.
    ↳ Think instead: one reason to change, meaning one actor. Group what changes together; separate what changes for different people.
  • "Open/closed means never modify existing code"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: "closed for modification" reads as a ban.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: bugs still get fixed in place, and no design is closed against every change. The principle is about new cases along an expected axis.
    ↳ Think instead: pick the axis the requirement names and make that one cheap. Everything else stays simple until it proves it varies.
  • "A square is a rectangle, so Square should extend Rectangle"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it is true in geometry, and "is-a" is taught as the test for inheritance.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the code's Rectangle promises independent width and height. Square breaks that, so correct code written for Rectangle returns 16 where it expects 20.
    ↳ Think instead: subtyping is about behaviour, not vocabulary. Ask whether every caller of the parent still works.
  • Not the same: dependency inversion vs dependency injection vs a DI container
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: same initials, and Spring made all three look like one feature.
    ↳ Difference: inversion is the principle (depend on an abstraction you own); injection is the technique (receive it through the constructor); a container automates the wiring.
    ↳ Think instead: in an LLD round you need the first two and plain constructors. No framework, no annotations.
  • Don't inject an interface that has exactly one implementation and no test fake.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: "program to an interface" sounds like a rule to apply everywhere.
    ↳ What goes wrong: every class gains a twin interface, navigation doubles, and nothing is more flexible than before.
    ↳ Do instead: add the interface at real boundaries: I/O, external services, and anything the requirement says will vary.
  • Don't recite definitions when asked about SOLID.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the acronym invites a five-item list.
    ↳ What goes wrong: the question in a design round is diagnostic ("which principle does this break?"), and definitions don't answer it.
    ↳ Do instead: name the tell you see in the code, the principle, and the fix, in that order.

Connections

  • Before this — OOP: the four pillars. SOLID is five disciplines on those four tools.
  • The counterweight — DRY, KISS, YAGNI: when not to add the abstraction SOLID suggests.
  • Recognition drill, one violation per letter — SOLID, with a violation each.
  • O, in depth — open/closed as the scoring rubric; the pattern it usually becomes is strategy.
  • I and D, in depth — interface segregation for extension points · constructor dependency injection.
  • L's usual fix — composition over inheritance.
  • From a requirement to the right seam — the pattern selector.

notes.title: DRY, KISS, YAGNI — Keeping a Design Small

headings.text: 1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)
6. YAGNI — build it when it's needed
7. When they pull against each other

notes.html:
This note has one job: give you three brakes to apply while designing. SOLID tells you where to add structure; these three tell you when to stop. A design round is lost as often by over-building as by under-building.

Reference Links

  • YAGNI, and the four costs of building early — Martin Fowler: Yagni
  • When removing duplication goes wrong — Sandi Metz: The Wrong Abstraction
  • The four rules of simple design — Martin Fowler: BeckDesignRules
  • DRY, as originally stated — Don't repeat yourself (from Hunt and Thomas, The Pragmatic Programmer)

REVISION BLOCK

1. Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
DRY, precisely? Every piece of knowledge has one authoritative home. It is about rules, not about text that looks alike.
KISS? The simplest design that meets today's stated requirements. Simple means few moving parts, not few lines.
YAGNI? Don't build a capability until a real requirement needs it.
When is duplication the better choice? When two pieces look alike by coincidence and will change for different reasons.
How does YAGNI square with open/closed? Add the seam where the requirement names a variation; don't build implementations nobody asked for.
Draw by hand: "should I add this abstraction?" Same knowledge or same text? → asked for, or seen three times? → can it be one function or one interface?

2. Interview Explanation (30 Seconds)

Three rules keep a design from growing faster than its requirements. DRY: each business rule lives in one place, so a change is one edit. KISS: choose the simplest design that satisfies what was asked. YAGNI: don't build for requirements that haven't arrived. They also limit each other: removing duplication too early creates a wrong abstraction, which is worse than the duplication. So I extract when the same rule appears a third time or the requirement names the variation, and not before.

3. At a glance

Says The tell that it's violated What over-applying it looks like
DRY · Don't Repeat Yourself one rule, one home a rule change needs the same edit in several files, and one gets missed unrelated code forced through one function with flags and special cases
KISS · Keep It Simple fewest moving parts that meet the requirement a newcomer can't trace one request without opening ten files cramming everything into one clever method
YAGNI · You Aren't Gonna Need It build it when it is needed parameters, options and layers no current feature uses refusing an obvious seam and paying for a rewrite a week later

The three meet in one decision that comes up constantly: should I add this abstraction?

The first question is DRY, the second is YAGNI, the third is KISS.

4. DRY — one rule, one home

The question it answers: when this rule changes, how many places do I have to edit?

The definition matters: every piece of knowledge must have a single, unambiguous, authoritative representation within a system. The word is knowledge. DRY is about business rules, formulas, schemas and decisions. It is not about making code that looks similar disappear.

A real violation. GST is computed in the cart preview and again on the invoice:

class CartPreview { long total(long subtotal) { return subtotal + subtotal * 18 / 100; } }
class Invoice     { long total(long subtotal) { return subtotal + subtotal * 18 / 100; } }

The rate changes; someone updates the invoice and forgets the preview; customers now see one total and are charged another. The rule existed in two places, so it could disagree with itself. The fix gives the rule one home:

final class Gst {
    static final int RATE_PERCENT = 18;
    static long on(long paise) { return paise * RATE_PERCENT / 100; }
    private Gst() {}
}
class CartPreview { long total(long subtotal) { return subtotal + Gst.on(subtotal); } }
class Invoice     { long total(long subtotal) { return subtotal + Gst.on(subtotal); } }
// both → 11800 for a subtotal of 10000

GST_RATE_PERCENT = 18

def gst(paise: int) -> int:                 # the rule lives here and nowhere else
    return paise * GST_RATE_PERCENT // 100

def cart_preview_total(subtotal: int) -> int: return subtotal + gst(subtotal)
def invoice_total(subtotal: int) -> int:      return subtotal + gst(subtotal)

Not a violation. Free shipping starts at ₹500 and loyalty points also start at ₹500:

class Shipping { static final long FREE_ABOVE_PAISE = 50_000; }
class Loyalty  { static final long POINTS_ABOVE_PAISE = 50_000; }

Same number, two different rules owned by two different teams. Merge them into one constant and the day marketing raises the loyalty threshold, shipping changes too. The test is not "do they look the same?" but "if one changes, must the other?"

The rule of three. Write it once. Write it twice and notice. On the third occurrence, extract, because by then you can see what really is common. Extract earlier and you guess the shape of the abstraction from two examples, and the third case arrives as a boolean parameter. Sandi Metz's line is the one to remember: duplication is far cheaper than the wrong abstraction.

DRY also applies beyond code: a validation rule repeated in the UI, the API and the database; a schema described in code and again in a document. Where a rule must appear in two layers, generate one from the other or name one as the owner.

5. KISS — the fewest moving parts

The question it answers: is this the simplest thing that meets the requirement in front of me?

The requirement: email the customer a receipt. An over-built answer:

// one requirement, five types, and a lookup by string
interface NotificationChannel { }
abstract class AbstractNotificationChannelFactory { }
class ChannelRegistry { /* Map<String, AbstractNotificationChannelFactory> */ }
class TemplateEngineProvider { }
class NotificationOrchestrator { /* resolves "EMAIL" → factory → channel → template → send */ }

Nothing here is wrong in itself. It is wrong for this requirement: there is one channel and one message, and five types to read before you find the line that sends it. The simple answer:

interface ReceiptSender { void send(String email, long totalPaise); }

class EmailReceiptSender implements ReceiptSender {
    public void send(String email, long totalPaise) {
        System.out.println("to " + email + ": total " + totalPaise);
    }
}
// → to a@b.in: total 11800

def send_receipt(email: str, total_paise: int) -> None:   # in Python, a function is enough
    print(f"to {email}: total {total_paise}")

One interface is kept in the Java version because sending email is a boundary to the outside world, and a test needs to replace it. That is the only abstraction with a reason today.

Simple is not the same as short or easy. A one-line nested stream with three lambdas is short and hard to read. Simple means few concepts and few connections between them: a reader can hold the whole thing in their head. Kent Beck's four rules of simple design give an order to check: it passes the tests, it reveals its intention, it has no duplicated knowledge, and it has the fewest elements. Fewest comes last: clarity outranks brevity.

In a design round, KISS has a practical form: start with the plainest classes that satisfy the stated use cases, and let the interviewer's follow-up pull the abstraction out of you. A candidate who opens with a factory, a registry and three patterns has nowhere to go when asked "now add X".

6. YAGNI — build it when it's needed

The question it answers: who asked for this?

// "we might go international one day"
long checkout(Order order, Currency currency, TaxRegion region,
              List<Plugin> plugins, Map<String, Object> featureFlags) { ... }

The shop sells in one country in one currency. Every one of those parameters has to be passed, tested, documented and understood by everyone who reads the method, starting today, for a need that may never come. Fowler names four costs of building a feature early:

Cost What you pay
Build the time spent building something not yet needed
Delay the wanted feature that shipped later because of it
Carry every later change is harder, because the extra code is in the way
Repair when the need finally arrives, it differs from the guess, so the early version is reworked anyway

The last one is what makes YAGNI more than thrift: you usually guess the future requirement wrong, because you don't yet know what it is.

What YAGNI does not forbid. It is about features and capabilities, not about keeping code easy to change. Clean names, small classes, tests and injected dependencies are not speculative; they are what make it cheap to add the feature later. So:

Speculative: leave it out Cheap seam: fine to keep
a multi-currency pricing engine, with one currency an OrderRepository interface, because storage is external and tests need a fake
a plugin system with no plugins a DiscountPolicy interface, when the requirement says "gold and silver members"
configuration options nobody sets a constructor parameter in place of a hard-coded new

7. When they pull against each other

Tension What goes wrong How to settle it
DRY vs KISS removing every repetition produces a shared helper with flags, harder to follow than the copies prefer a little duplication to an abstraction with parameters that switch its behaviour
DRY vs YAGNI extracting on the second occurrence, guessing at the third the rule of three
YAGNI vs open/closed SOLID says add an extension point; YAGNI says you don't need it yet add the seam (an interface) where the requirement states a plural or there is an external boundary; don't add implementations nobody asked for
KISS vs SOLID in general an interface per class "for flexibility" each abstraction must name the change it makes cheap. If you can't name it, remove it

One sentence covers all four: an abstraction is justified by a requirement you can point to, either one that is stated, or one you have already met three times. In an interview the requirement you can point to is usually the plural the interviewer just said: "card, UPI or wallet".

8. Interview Follow-ups

Q · Mechanism — Two methods have identical bodies. Is that a DRY violation?

Not necessarily. DRY is about knowledge, so the question is whether they encode the same rule. If both compute GST, they must always agree, and having two copies means they can drift: that is a violation, and the rule gets one home. If one computes a shipping threshold and the other a loyalty threshold that happen to share a value, they are different rules that will change for different reasons. Merging them couples two teams' decisions. The test I apply is: if one of these changes, is it a bug for the other not to change?

Q · Trade-off — Your design has an interface for pricing with one implementation. The interviewer asks if that's over-engineering.

It depends on what the requirement said. If it mentioned weekday and weekend pricing, or member tiers, the variation is stated and the interface is where the follow-up will land, so it stays, and I would say that out loud. If pricing was a single fixed rule and I added the interface from habit, it is speculative and I would inline it. The cost of adding it later is small: extracting an interface from one concrete class is a quick, safe refactor. External boundaries such as storage and payment are the exception; they get an interface regardless, because tests need to replace them.

Q · Failure — A shared calculateTotal(order, isRefund, isB2B, skipTax, legacyMode) has grown five boolean flags. What happened, and what do you do?

It began as a sensible extraction of duplicated code, and then each new caller needed something slightly different, so a flag was added in place of questioning the abstraction. Now every caller pays for every other caller's special case, and nobody can change it safely. Confirm by listing which flag combinations are actually used; usually it is three or four. The fix is to go backwards first: inline the function into each caller, delete what that caller doesn't use, and then see what is truly common. What remains is usually a small core plus separate, plainly named functions.

Q · Design — You have 45 minutes to design a parking lot. How do these three shape what you build?

KISS sets the starting point: the plainest classes for the stated use cases (lot, floor, spot, ticket, a fee calculation) with in-memory storage. YAGNI decides what I name and exclude out loud: no payments, no reservations, no multi-lot support unless asked. DRY keeps each rule in one place, most importantly the fee rule and the spot-allocation rule, since those are what follow-ups change. I add an interface only at those two points and at storage, because the requirement mentions vehicle types and pricing that varies. Scoping is covered in deliberate scope cuts.

Pitfalls

  • "DRY means never write the same code twice"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the name says "don't repeat yourself", and duplicate lines are easy to see.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the principle is about duplicated knowledge. Code that matches by coincidence, merged into one function, ties together things that change for different reasons.
    ↳ Think instead: ask "if one changes, must the other?" If no, the duplication is harmless and the merge is the bug.
  • "Duplication is always worse than an abstraction"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: extracting feels like cleaning up, and reviewers praise it.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: an abstraction guessed from two examples gets a flag for the third and another for the fourth, until nobody can change it. Undoing it is harder than the copies ever were.
    ↳ Think instead: duplication is far cheaper than the wrong abstraction. Wait for the third occurrence, and inline again if the shape turns out wrong.
  • "KISS means the least code"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: shorter looks simpler, and a clever one-liner feels elegant.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: simplicity is about how many ideas a reader must hold at once, not about line count. Dense code can be short and hard.
    ↳ Think instead: simple means few moving parts and an obvious path from input to output. Clear beats clever, and clear beats short.
  • "YAGNI means don't design for the future at all"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: "you aren't gonna need it" sounds like a ban on thinking ahead.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: it targets speculative features. Readable names, tests and injected dependencies aren't features; they are what make later change cheap.
    ↳ Think instead: keep the code easy to change, and build the capability on the day it is asked for.
  • Don't open a design round with patterns.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: showing a factory, a strategy and an observer early feels like showing depth.
    ↳ What goes wrong: the model is hard to explain, takes the whole session to write, and has no slack when the follow-up arrives.
    ↳ Do instead: start plain, and introduce each abstraction at the moment a requirement or follow-up asks for it, naming that requirement.
  • Don't use YAGNI to skip an interface at an external boundary.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: there is only one database today, so the interface looks speculative.
    ↳ What goes wrong: the business logic can't be tested without the real thing, and that cost starts immediately, not in the future.
    ↳ Do instead: put an interface around storage, payment, time and network calls from the start. The second implementation already exists: the in-memory fake in your tests.

Connections

  • What these three restrain — SOLID, which says where to add structure; and OOP: the four pillars, the tools it adds structure with.
  • The same warning, for patterns — pattern overuse and the catalogue's anti-patterns.
  • YAGNI at the start of a round — deliberate scope cuts · in-memory-first rule.
  • Where a seam is justified — open/closed as the scoring rubric and the pattern selector: the plural in the requirement is the evidence.

6. The three confusions that get probed 🔀
7. Before you name anything — the two gates
8. The sentence to say when you pick one

notes.html:
This note has one job: get you from the sentence the interviewer just said to one pattern, in under ten seconds, without walking a catalogue in your head.

The code-smell route — "I'm staring at this code, what's wrong with it?" — is already built at ../03-design-patterns/catalogue/decision-tree.md (Gate 0, three branches, cost ledger, reverse check). Don't duplicate it; this is the other door into the same house. In the LLD round you have no code yet — you have a requirement being read aloud, and you have to choose before you type.

Reference Links

  • The code-smell tree (use when refactoring) — ../03-design-patterns/catalogue/decision-tree.md
  • Pattern catalogue — creational · structural · behavioral
  • The LLD-round layer per pattern — ../03-design-patterns/ (items 14–26)
  • Why "now add X" is the whole rubric — ../02-oo-design-principles/07-open-closed-as-the-scoring-rubric.md

REVISION BLOCK

1. Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What do you listen for in the requirement? The plural. "Card, UPI or wallet", "gold/silver members", "SMS and email" — plurality is the axis of change.
The one question that picks the pattern? What will they ask me to add in ten minutes? The pattern is whatever makes that addition a new file, not an edit.
Why not decide from the code? In LLD there is no code yet. You get one sentence, and the design is scored on the follow-up it survives.
What do you say out loud when you pick one? Friction → pattern → cost, unprompted. Volunteering the cost is the staff-level tell.

2. Interview Explanation (30 Seconds)

I don't pick patterns from a catalogue — I pick them from the requirement's grammar. A plural noun ("card, UPI, wallet") means a policy varies, so that's Strategy behind an interface I own. A lifecycle ("requested → assigned → completed") means behaviour varies per stage, so that's State. An "and also, and also" list after an event ("on booking, send SMS and update search and email") means who reacts varies, so that's Observer. A vendor name in the sentence ("Stripe", "Twilio") means an Adapter at the boundary. Everything else is usually not a pattern yet — and saying that is worth more than naming one.

3. The selector — requirement grammar → pattern

Those six carry the round. The remaining items are reached for while writing the classes, not while hearing the requirement — second chart below.

4. The six, as a lookup

What you hear What actually varies Pattern The follow-up it absorbs
"…by card, UPI or wallet" · "flat, hourly or surge" A policy Strategy 🔴 "Now add weekend pricing / nearest-car matching" — new class, zero edits
"requested → assigned → in-ride → completed" · "held, confirmed, expired" Behaviour per stage State 🔴 "What if it's cancelled mid-ride?" — a transition, not a new if
"when a booking is made, notify the driver and update inventory and email" Who reacts Observer 🔴 "Also push to analytics" — a new listener; publisher untouched
"integrate with Stripe / Twilio / the provider's SDK" The boundary Adapter 🟢 "Support a third provider" — one PaymentGateway we own, one adapter each
"toppings" · "add-ons" · "insurance on top of the fare" Composable extras Decorator 🟡 "Combine two add-ons" — wrap twice, no 2ⁿ subclasses
"validate, then check the rate limit, then authorize" The pipeline CoR 🟡 "Insert a fraud check before authorize" — one more handler

The plural is the whole trick. Strategy, State and Observer are ~80% of what an LLD round wants. If you can hear which of the three a sentence is, you have already passed the design half of the round.

5. The other six — reached for while writing, not while listening

6. The three confusions that get probed

Asked as The one-line separator
Strategy vs State Both are "an interface with implementations." Strategy is handed in from outside and never changes itself; State replaces itself on a transition. If the object decides its own next mode, it's State. (item 18)
Strategy vs Template Method Strategy varies a whole algorithm by composition, swappable at runtime. Template Method fixes the step order in a final method and varies steps by inheritance — compile-time only. Two independently varying steps → a subclass per combination → use Strategy. (item 22)
Adapter vs Facade vs Decorator vs Proxy Identical shape, four intents: Adapter = compatibility (make theirs look like mine) · Facade = simplicity (fewer calls) · Decorator = enhancement (same interface, more behaviour) · Proxy = control (client doesn't know you're there). Matching on "it's a wrapper" instead of on intent is the classic tell. (item 24)

7. Before you name anything — the two gates

  1. Has it changed twice, or is the change on the table? One occurrence is a coincidence. An interface with one implementation and no second in sight is cost, not design. (Full Gate 0: decision-tree.md)
  2. Would a lambda, a record, a Map or an enum do it? A lambda is a Strategy. Map<Key, Supplier<T>> is a Factory. An enum with behaviour is a small State machine. In a 60-minute round the lighter form scores the same and costs you five minutes less. Say: "I'd start with an enum here; if per-state behaviour grows, this becomes the State pattern."

Naming a pattern you can't justify is a negative signal — see ../03-design-patterns/26-pattern-overuse.md. "This doesn't need a pattern yet" is a senior answer.

8. The sentence to say when you pick one

Friction → pattern → cost. "Right now, adding a payment provider means editing PaymentService.charge(). I'll put the provider behind a PaymentGateway interface we own, so a new provider is a new adapter plus a registry entry. The cost is one indirection — you can't see the concrete provider from the call site, so I'll log the selected one."

Step three, volunteered without being asked, is what separates read the GoF book from maintained this for two years.
